Find the polar coordinates for the intersection points of the circles $r=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ and $r=\sqrt{3},$ shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
To determine the polar coordinates of the intersection points, we will solve the following system of equations for $r$ and $\theta :$  

$$
\{\begin{aligned}r=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ r=\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

We begin by setting the equations equal to each other and solve for $\theta .$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =\sqrt{3} \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this equation in the interval $[0,2\pi ),$ we obtain ${\theta }_{1}=\frac{4\pi }{3}$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\frac{5\pi }{3}$ .

Also, notice that $r=\sqrt{3}$ at both intersection points.

Therefore, polar coordinates of the points of intersection are 

$\,$ $(r,\theta )=(\sqrt{3},\frac{4\pi }{3})\,$ and $\,(r,\theta )=(\sqrt{3},\frac{5\pi }{3}).$

$$

This gives us the solution $\theta ={315}^{∘}$ in the $4$th quadrant.

Now, we use the equation $r=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ to find the $r$-coordinate of the point $A:$  

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡({315}^{∘}) \\  & =2\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the polar coordinates of the point $A$ are 

$\,$ $(r,\theta )=(\sqrt{2},{315}^{∘}).$

questions.worked_solution:
To determine the polar coordinates of the intersection points, we will solve the following system of equations for $r$ and $\theta :$  

$$
\{\begin{aligned}r=3-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ r=4+3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

We begin by setting the equations equal to each other and solve for $\theta .$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}3-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =4+3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 5\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =-1 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =-\frac{1}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this equation in the interval $[{0}^{∘},{360}^{∘}),$ we obtain ${\theta }_{1}≈{191.5}^{∘}$ and ${\theta }_{2}≈348.5,$ rounded to $1$ decimal place. 

Now, we use the equation $r=4+3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ to find the $r$-coordinates of the intersection points: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{1} & =4+3\operatorname{sin}⁡{\theta }_{1}=4+3\cdot (-\frac{1}{5})=\frac{17}{5}=3.4 \\ {r}_{2} & =4+3\operatorname{cos}⁡{\theta }_{2}=4+3\cdot (-\frac{1}{5})=\frac{17}{5}=3.4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, polar coordinates of the points of intersection are

$\,$ $(r,\theta )≈(3.4,{191.5}^{∘})\,$ and $\,(r,\theta )≈(3.4,{348.5}^{∘}).$

questions.problem: The curves $r=2-3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ and $r=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ for $\theta \in [0,2\pi )$ intersect at a single point in the second quadrant. Determine the polar coordinates of this point.
questions.worked_solution:
To determine the polar coordinates of the intersection points, we will solve the following system of equations for $r$ and $\theta :$  

$$
\{\begin{aligned}r=2-3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ r=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

We begin by setting the equations equal to each other and solve for $\theta .$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2-3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =2 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this equation in the interval $[0,2\pi ),$ we obtain ${\theta }_{1}=\frac{\pi }{6}$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\frac{5\pi }{6}.$

Therefore, the $\theta $-coordinate of the point that we're interested in is $\theta =\frac{5\pi }{6},$ since it lies in the second quadrant.

Now, we use the equation $r=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ to find the $r$-coordinate of our point:

$$
r=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{6})=\frac{1}{2}
$$

Therefore, the polar coordinates of the desired intersection point are

$\,$ $(r,\theta )=(\frac{1}{2},\frac{5\pi }{6}).$

canonical_examples.problem:
The circles $r=4\cos \theta$ and $r=4\sqrt{3}\sin  \theta$ intersect at points $O$ and $A,$ as shown in the diagram. What are the polar coordinates of the point $A?$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14226602/assets/2766090535f1931a0cb15a248eb62c9b1dc5b5f9bc15b6dff5d544876527d77c.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First of all, we notice from the graph that $(r,\theta)=\left(0, 0\right)$ is an obvious first point of intersection. 

To find the second point of intersection, we set the equations of the curves equal to each other and solve for $\theta\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}4\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta } & =\frac{4}{4\sqrt{3}} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡\theta  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us the solution $\theta =\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ in the $1$st quadrant.

Now, we use the equation $r=4\cos \theta$ to find the $r$-coordinate of the point $A\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =4\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}) \\  & =4\cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\  & =2\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, polar coordinates of the point $A$ are $(r,\theta)=\left(2\sqrt{3}, \dfrac{\pi}{6}\right).$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To determine the polar coordinates of the intersection points, we will solve the following system of equations for $r$ and $\theta\mathbin{:}$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}r=3+3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ r=4\end{aligned}
$$

We begin by setting the equations equal to each other and solving for $\theta.$ This gives

$$
\eqalign{
		3+3\cos \theta & = 4\[5pt]
 	 	3\cos \theta & = 1   \[3pt]
 		\cos \theta & = \dfrac 1 3.
	}
$$

Solving this equation in the interval $[0^\circ,360^\circ),$ we obtain $\theta_1 \approx 70.5^{\circ}$ and $\theta_2 \approx 289.5,$ rounded to $1$ decimal place.

Notice that we must have 
$r=4$
 at any of the points of intersection.

Therefore, the polar coordinates of the points of intersection are

$$
(r,\theta)=\left(4 , 70.5 \, ^\circ \right)\qquad \textrm{and} \qquad (r,\theta)=\left(4 , 289.5 \, ^\circ\right).
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
It is often more convenient to use polar coordinates to determine the points of intersection of two curves. This is especially true if we are dealing with two circles. 

Suppose, for example, that we are given the circles ${\color{}r=\sqrt2\,  {\sin{\theta}}}\,$ and $\, {\color{}r=1},$ as shown in the figure below. How do we determine  the polar coordinates of the points of intersection of these two curves?  

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14226602/assets/8225490259dfcf03d505b7f68a486a8246a46b29f6047f1c066d0e9436f8b55f.png)

 

To determine the polar coordinates of the intersection points, we must solve the following system of equations for $r$ and $\theta\mathbin{:}$  

$$
\{\begin{aligned}r=\sqrt{2}\text{ }\,\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ r=1\end{aligned}
$$

So, we begin by setting the equations equal to each other and solving for $\theta.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{2}\text{ }\,\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this equation in the interval $[0,2\pi),$ we obtain 

$$
\theta_1 = \dfrac{\pi}{4}, \qquad \theta_2 = \dfrac{3\pi}{4}.
$$

Also, notice that $r=1$ at both intersection points. Therefore, the polar coordinates of the points of intersection are 

$$
(r,\theta)=\bigg(1, \dfrac{\pi}{4}\bigg)\qquad \textrm{and} \qquad(r,\theta)=\bigg(1, \dfrac{3\pi}{4}\bigg).
$$
